awd_titl_txt: I-Corps: Translation Potential of Micromachined Electrostatic Cooling Fans
awd_abstract_narration:
This I-Corps project focuses on the development of a new class of chip-scale cooling micro-fans. Effective heat removal (cooling) continues to be a major bottleneck for achieving higher processing power in large scale integrated digital electronics. As electronics like smartphones, laptops, and medical devices get smaller and more powerful, they generate more heat in tighter spaces. This new technology provides powerful, silent, and compact cooling systems, helping devices run better and last longer without overheating. With the growing demand for artificial intelligence and consequently the need for ever-increasing higher processing powers and massive data centers, electronic cooling is also a growing challenge. This solution offers a chip-scale micro-fan that can be mounted directly on high performing electronic components, blowing a high velocity air stream onto the hot surface to provide a more efficient, effective, and compact solution. Successful commercialization of this technology may contribute to the growth of advanced chip manufacturing and data center capacity in the United States.  

This I-Corps project utilizes experiential learning coupled with a first-hand investigation of the industry ecosystem to assess the translation potential of the technology. This solution is based on the development of a tiny device, a chip-scale actuator, capable of producing up to ten-times more mechanical energy in the same amount of space compared to existing lead-based devices known as piezoelectric transducers. The technology works by using advanced three-dimensional silicon micro-manufacturing techniques to increase the surface area inside the silicon chip, which helps it create more energy. These devices can make tiny parts vibrate very fast: microscale cantilevers that vibrate at ultrasonic frequencies that humans can't hear, to power small air-blowers to become cooling micro-fans. This technology is important because it can cool small electronic devices more efficiently and in a much smaller space than current technology allows.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
The objective of this I-Corps project was to investigate the potential customer base and commercial viability of a new class of micro-machined chip-scale cooling fans.  This was be accomplished by participating in the vigorous I-Corps training and mentoring program in addition to conducting numerous (over 100) interviews with different experts, stakeholders and potential customers of the envisioned devices.

Effective heat removal (cooling) has been and continues to be a major bottleneck for achieving higher processing power in VLSI digital electronics (e.g. GPU, CPU, Memory, etc.) limited by their excessive heat generation (hence the need for inclusion of often noisy conventional rotary fans in desktop and laptop computers among others). With the growing demand for Artificial Intelligence (AI) and consequently the need for exponentially higher processing powers and massive data centers, electronic cooling is also a growing challenge. A chip-scale cooling fan that can be mounted directly on high performing electronic components blowing a high velocity air stream onto the hot surface, provides a more efficient, effective, and compact solution to this prevailing problem.

Overall, the feedback from the interviewed experts and stakeholders was positive indicating a clear need for the proposed compact air-cooling solution in the electronics industry.  Specifically there are various electronic components with power consumption in the few to tens of watts used in consumer electronics, data centers, wearable devices, etc. that are currently either not actively cooled, or cooled via the conventional bulky components such as rotary fans in combination with heat transfer passive components such as heat pipes, vapor chambers, etc.  Having a compact chip-scale active cooling device repelling the generated heat via forced air convection can improve the performance, or contribute significantly to higher levels of integration and compactness in the next generations of such systems.

The findings under this project encouraged the founding of a start-up company, by the team members to pursue development of chip-scale fans and their commercialization. The company has already attracted pre-seed private investment and has developed prototype designs that are currently being fabricated at a MEMS foundry.
